New guidance from Colorado officials says schools don’t need to verify whether a student is male or female to comply with a recently passed ballot initiative that aimed to bar transgender athletes from school sports teams aligned with their gender identity.

The guidance directs schools and districts not to inspect a student’s body, request photographs of a student’s body, ask for DNA or genetic testing, require physical exams to determine sex, require affidavits related to a student’s reproductive system, or question students about intimate medical information.

The Colorado Department of Education released the 6-page guidance document to schools and districts Wednesday, about six weeks before Proposition 134 is set to take effect on Jan. 1.

The guidance frees schools from the controversial task of verifying students’ sex when they join boys or girls sports teams, but it could anger backers of the ballot measure, which passed 52-48%. The guidance shows that state officials are not interpreting Proposition 134 in the same way as supporters.

While the ballot language didn’t specify how a student athlete’s sex was to be determined,…

items.title: New state dashboard reveals Colorado young people need more help connecting to college and careers
items.summary:
On Monday, Gov. Jared Polis unveiled a new data dashboard focused on young people’s career readiness, civic experiences, and personal well-being. It’s an initiative he pushed for during his time as chair of the National Governors Association.

The new scorecard shows the state scored a 21.14 out of 30 this year in the postsecondary and workforce category. When compared to data compiled from 2019, this is just a .17 increase. The tool tracks whether 18- to 24-year-olds have graduated with work experience or credentials, enrolled in postsecondary learning programs or are unemployed.

Polis has leaned into recent U.S. News and World Report rankings that say Colorado is ranked No. 1 in education, including when he announced the state’s Let’s Get Ready tool. But Polis’ own data reveals more needs to be done to help Colorado’s young people connect to the workforce, career training, or college.

Polis said the tool will help state officials identify areas that need more focus. He will leave office in January, and his administration has said the tool is fully customizable for the next governor to tweak.
items.t: New state dashboard reveals Colorado young people need more help connecting to college and careers

items.title: Job pipelines for Black and Latino students ‘dry up’ after attacks on DEI and affirmative action
items.summary:
This video story, by Soledad O’Brien Productions for TIME and The Hechinger Report, examines the consequences of the SCOTUS decision about affirmative action .

LOS ANGELES — Jamila Chambers remembers when recruiters came to interview students at Occidental College with a clear mission: They wanted a diverse workforce.

They interviewed juniors for internships that often led to full-time offers. Finance firms came and ran affinity information sessions and job shadowing programs for first- and second-year students.

“They would specifically say: ‘We’re looking for BIPOC students. We’re looking for first-gen students. We’re looking for LGBTQIA+ students,’” said Chambers, executive director of the school’s Hameetman Career Center.

Not anymore. Those pipelines, Chambers said, have “dried up.” 

After a divided Supreme Court gutted race-conscious admissions in 2023, colleges could no longer give an edge to Black and Latino applicants over white and Asian applicants in the name of diversity, ushering in a new era for higher education. That meant the end of policies aimed at turning around historically low representation and systemic discrimination. 

Affirmative Action 

This story is part of a series produced by The Hechinger Report and Soledad O’Brien Productions about the ongoing impact of the Supreme Court ruling. 

Read more 

The court’s ruling — which 2 out of 3 American adults said was “mostly a good thing” — did not address or change hiring laws nor mention employer efforts to make workplaces more inclusive.

Yet many employers have since dismantled existing efforts to…
items.t: Job pipelines for Black and Latino students ‘dry up’ after attacks on DEI and affirmative action

items.title: COLUMN: Will the blue wave reopen job opportunities for Black and Hispanic students?
items.summary:
WASHINGTON – Trinity Williams has some advice for prospective students visiting Howard University in the era since the Supreme Court banned colleges from considering race in admissions. 

“Always choose an HBCU,” Williams, a junior and tour guide at the historically Black university, told me on a recent October day, recounting the pep talk she loves to give to high schoolers. Howard, a top-ranked private research university, opened in 1867 to educate newly freed African Americans and train Black clergymen and teachers, and now boasts a range of iconic alumni and a built-in advice and support network Williams hopes to take advantage of.

“Our students are competing at a higher or a more elite level,” Williams said. “Companies, organizations, businesses — they know they can come to Howard and get students who are primed and mentored and crafted. I always encourage students of color to come to HBCUs.”

Trinity Williams, a tour guide at Howard University, shows visitors around campus. Credit: Liz Willen/The Hechinger Report 

I was struck by the optimism Williams feels about career prospects in a tough job market because my conversation with her followed months of reporting by The Hechinger Report and Soledad O’Brien Productions that found the opposite. In our ongoing series on the end of affirmative action, students and some career counselors we spoke with decried what they said was the disappearance of recruiting efforts on their campuses following the court’s decision, accelerated by subsequent executive orders from President Donald Trump banning diversity, equity and…
items.t: COLUMN: Will the blue wave reopen job opportunities for Black and Hispanic students?

items.title: Fewer students, more teachers: Districts balk at cutting staff even as enrollment falls
items.summary:
SEATTLE — Nearly four decades ago, state auditors delivered a stark warning to Seattle Public Schools.

The district needed to close several campuses with low enrollment to avert a deepening budget crisis. But the recommendations generated fierce neighborhood outcry, so Seattle officials set the audit aside.

Then, 34 years later, history repeated itself. In 2024, Seattle’s then-superintendent proposed shuttering up to a fifth of its schools because there weren’t enough students to fill them, but again scrapped the plan after community resistance. 

Now, the district’s back in the same financial bind, with opposition already building against a new plan to shutter nearly a dozen campuses.

The cycle in Seattle reflects what some education experts call a national paralysis in school district boardrooms. Public school enrollment has plummeted by more than 1.4 million students since the pandemic, according to a new study by Stanford University researchers Thomas Dee and Jaymes Pyne. That’s primarily due to declining birth rates and expanding school choice. Yet, rather than downsize to match their new financial reality, district leaders throughout the country have largely hesitated.

One out of every 4 public schools in the U.S. has lost 15 percent or more of its student population since 2019, according to the study. (In Seattle, enrollment has fallen by roughly 8 percent since that year, to below 49,000 students.) Despite these empty desks, the overall number of schools in operation remains virtually unchanged — and teacher headcounts have actually grown by 1 percent…
items.t: Fewer students, more teachers: Districts balk at cutting staff even as enrollment falls

Chicago Public Schools and its principals union have reached a tentative deal on a historic three-year contract that would be the first comprehensive union contract for public school principals in Illinois.

The district and union signed an interim deal last fall that gave school leaders raises and included protections against harassment and more due process for those facing discipline. But they continued to bargain on a range of issues. After roughly two years of negotiations, the union’s principal and assistant principal members are voting this week to ratify the full contract. The agreement also needs approval from the school board, likely at its December meeting.

items.title: Preschool math blasts off in Mississippi
items.summary:
CORINTH, Miss. — Vaughn Dodd is using Magna-Tiles to make a rocketship, carefully selecting different shapes for the nose cone and the tail. The four-year-old pre-K student at Corinth Elementary School knows that a diamond shape is called a rhombus. She knows the sun is a circle. 

Proficiency with translucent plastic shapes may not lead directly to a future job in Mississippi’s growing aerospace industry, but it’s not a bad launching pad for any number of careers that involve mathematical concepts.

Vaughn’s teacher, Kayla Wood, leads a range of activities in the name of math, some with the whole class and some in small groups. Toys like the Magna-Tiles, which support counting, sorting and other skills, are available for independent play. 

“There are no worksheets here,” Wood said. “We don’t do worksheets at any time, even during literacy. We can form letters and numbers with Play-Doh. It’s very hands-on.”

Wood is implementing Building Blocks, the math component of the Mississippi Beginnings curriculum for state-funded pre-K programs. Mississippi is the first state to mandate a math curriculum for its preschool program, which currently serves around 8,700 children, or a quarter of the state’s population of four-year-olds. The rollout of the program started in 2022 and is expected to be in all state-funded preschools by August 2027.

Kayla Wood and her students during a morning of learning at Kossuth Elementary. Starting in the 2027-28 school year, every state-funded pre-K program in Mississippi will be required to use a common early childhood math curriculum called…
items.t: Preschool math blasts off in Mississippi

items.title: Students want hands-on training in the work of democracy. Colleges are answering
items.summary:
KENOSHA, Wis. — Andrew Staff knew the data. The sophomore at the University of Wisconsin-Madison had helped create an information packet for the 26 residents of Kenosha County, each randomly selected and paid $100 to spend a Saturday confronting the local housing crunch. The key question: Could factory-built dwellings help? 

But by the end of the six-hour session, during which residents raised and wrestled with one another’s concerns, Staff’s head was spinning. Affordability was just one factor, he noted, ticking off others such as proximity to parks and transportation and the fact that not every resident actually wants their own house. 

Days later, Staff switched his major from political science to public policy, newly offered this fall at the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s La Follette School of Public Affairs, which had helped organize the Kenosha event in part to give students real-world experience. 

UW-Madison sophomore Andrew Staff, who helped prepare background materials for housing assembly, talks with participants during the session. Darren Hauck for The Hechinger Report 

“I don’t just want to think about political theory,” said Staff. “I want to get out there and do things.” 

It’s no secret that Gen Z is unhappy with the direction of the country , distrustful of government and concerned about political polarization. But there’s also evidence they want to do something about it: Seventy-nine percent of those polled in April 2026 felt they could make a difference by voting and participating in the democratic process; 38 percent want to run for state or local…
items.t: Students want hands-on training in the work of democracy. Colleges are answering

items.title: States step up their role picking winners among college majors and training programs

For years, higher education policy has focused on getting more Americans into college and helping more of them graduate. Now the emphasis has shifted to another question: What are students and the general public getting out of these degrees?

Colleges are being pressed to show that their graduates find good jobs and earn enough to justify the cost of their education. And as criticism of higher education mounts, colleges face additional pressure to show that they are fueling their regional economies.

State policymakers are responding. Both red and blue states are stepping up their efforts to identify which fields are most needed for producing future workers and using those lists to steer subsidies to academic programs — everything from short-term training to graduate school. 

A new 50-state report released today by HCM Strategists, a firm that advises on and advocates for higher education policies, documents how states are identifying high-priority fields of study. It’s something of a central planning exercise, trying to predict what will be needed in the future. Some states rely on labor-market data, including wages and projections of occupational growth. Others use human judgment and advice from employers and industry experts. Still others combine the two.

The stakes are high. Roughly half the states incorporate their priority lists into funding formulas, giving colleges additional money for producing degrees in designated fields. Thirty-five states help pay for the costs of starting up a new degree program in high-priority fields.

items.t: States step up their role picking winners among college majors and training programs

items.title: How a class on climate change leaves students feeling ‘energized’
items.summary:
Jeffrey Seidman holds a doctorate in philosophy. He spent much of his first two decades as a college professor helping students interpret texts by writers like Aristotle, Plato and Kant. And yet Seidman, of Vassar College, also teaches one of the most compelling classes on climate change I’ve come across.

The course, Climate Solutions and Climate Careers: Finding Your Place in the Climate Fight , teaches students about the technologies, policies and strategies behind the clean energy transition, and how to advance them. It’s built on the idea that virtually every career — in fields as diverse as law, finance, education and urban planning — can play a role in combating the climate crisis. 

Students spend two classes per week studying solutions, such as electrifying transportation, greening the grid and bringing clean energy to the developing world. On Fridays, they hear from an outside speaker whose career is devoted to advancing climate solutions. Past speakers have included Emma Fisher, co-founder of Climate Cabinet, which backs candidates for local and state office who are supportive of climate action, and Zoe Samuel, a venture partner at Starshot Capital, which invests in climate technology like ultra-efficient heat pumps and food additives to reduce livestock methane emissions. Seidman also runs a website to bring lessons from his class to a wider audience. 

I recently spoke with Seidman about his course, which he has taught since 2021. At the end of our conversation, he issued a sort of call to arms to other liberal arts professors to step outside of their…
items.t: How a class on climate change leaves students feeling ‘energized’
